book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

chapters.file: ch21 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Uses Paul Ricoeur's distinction between idem-identity (sameness) and ipse-identity (selfhood) to dissolve the paradox of Tara's lower-back tattoo: she is bodily the same Dr. Knowles yet disavows the 19-year-old who got it, identity being the narrative that weaves the two together. Tig's mushroom-fueled apology to a doll and his 'I don't know who I am anymore' after killing Donna show character as the set of lasting dispositions by which we are recognized, while Opie's competing promises to Donna and SAMCRO anchor self-constancy up to his 'I got this' sacrifice for Jax. It closes with John Teller's manuscript as a narrative identity that receives no closure even in death — a just institution aiming at 'the good life with and for others' whose story Jax continues.

chapters.file: ch22 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Reads Jax's '92 miles an hour' monologue in 'Sovereign' through Heidegger and Hubert Dreyfus: expert riding, Chibs's pub brawling, and Tara's surgery are pre-reflective embodied skills that conscious rule-following would only ruin. Tig fixing bikes in the Teller-Morrow garage illustrates readiness-to-hand, Bobby's smoke-spewing Fat Boy the breakdown of un-readiness-to-hand, and browsing the Harley parts catalogue the detached present-at-hand. Against the alienation of calculative, instrumental thinking (Marx, Heidegger's standing-reserve — Clay selling the club to the Galindo Cartel, Cara Cara's porn bodies), the chapter follows Pirsig: maintenance is a form of care, so Opie rebuilding a '65 Panhead after Donna's death reconciles the biker with technology instead of enslaving him to it.

chapters.file: ch23 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
ch24 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Sets up Sons of Anarchy as a Hamlet retelling — Jax the prince, Clay the Claudius who murdered John Teller and married Gemma, Tara a gutsier Ophelia — and reads it through Freud and Ernest Jones's Hamlet and Oedipus: Jax's protest that he 'untwisted my mommy thing a long time ago,' his toleration of Gemma's meddling, and the Season 4/5 finale tableaux where Gemma displaces Tara at his side betray an unresolved Oedipus complex. Freud's three agencies get bodies: Clay as pure Id (beating Gemma in 'Hands'), Tara as Superego, Jax as the mediating Ego, with SAMCRO itself a collective Id worshipped in its 'chapel.' Oral and anal-stage fixations explain the Sons' chain-smoking, recklessness, and defiance of authority, while the Id's civil war between libido and the death drive plays out in Gemma's post-beating sex binge and Jax's unconscious pleasure in killing.

chapters.file: ch25 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Applies Luce Irigaray's account of patriarchal society to Charming's women: Gemma and Tara are strong and resourceful, but their identity, power, and even survival run through men, as Clay's 'you are NOT a member of this club — you're just an old lady!' and Jax's 'She's just an old lady, not a member' make brutally literal. Irigaray's claim that patriarchal orders circulate women as commodities exchanged among men fits the 'sweet butt' Cherry being offered to Clay in 'Patch Over' and Gemma's 'Only men need to feel loved. Women need to feel wanted.' Tara's sacrificed surgical career and Jax's refusal to live off his wife ('I'm not gonna live off my wife. I can't.') illustrate woman as a being who exists for another, and the chapter ends asking what Gemma could say if she had a genuinely feminine voice of her own.

chapters.file: ch26 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Frames the show's tension between the masculine public sphere (the chapel table, guns, club politics) and the feminine domestic sphere that actually sustains life, using Aristotle's oikos/polis division and Arendt's The Human Condition on the public/private realms. Gemma, dismissed as 'just an old lady,' proves the private sphere's power: she brought the club to Charming, orchestrates Jax's rise to the presidency, and converts her rape by Weston's LOAN goons into family solidarity that puts Jax's VP patch back on. Gilligan's and Baier's ethics of care then reads Lyla's abortion as a caring choice about family size, Tara's 'my job as your old lady is to be strong when and where you can't be' as care turned to strength, and Gemma's care curdling into retributive justice against Clay.

chapters.file: ch27 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
ch28 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Treats SAMCRO as the 'Sons of History': Hesiod's ages of decline fit the fall from the First 9's 1967 golden-age founding to the 'Age of Clay,' and Vico's corsi e recorsi explains how Clay's rational greed — muling cocaine for the Galindo Cartel — is the 'barbarism of reflection' that follows the loss of J.T.'s founding imagination. Christian providential history is tried against the show itself (Jax sleeping at the 'Patmos' mausoleum, 'The Revelator') but set aside for Hegel: Jax is the dialectical synthesis of thesis J.T. and antithesis Clay, keeping his father's ideals while acquiring Clay's cold cunning, which is how he outplays June Stahl and Damon Pope. Piney's counsel that Jax must 'find' his father before moving on makes the Delphic 'know thyself' the engine of the club's progress.

chapters.file: ch29 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Weighs Marx against Heidegger on whether SAMCRO should fight its history. Teller-Morrow read as petit-bourgeois capitalism turns the Mayans' pilot-episode raid into industrial sabotage and Nero's escort business into exploitation; read through Proudhon, Kropotkin, and Emma Goldman — whose essay John Teller found quoted on a Nevada wall — the club is an anarcho-syndicalist commune with democratic chapel votes, Kropotkin's mutual aid to widows like Lyla, and Tara as its socialized healthcare. Heidegger's historicity gives the resolution: Jax cannot escape the past (the Irish deal only with Clay; 'The sting of that betrayal ain't gonna fade') but can appropriate it authentically, and Pope's forced choice of a victim in 'Laying Pipe' confronts him with being-toward-death.

chapters.file: ch30 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Argues the Sons' value system is strikingly Homeric: like the warriors of the Iliad and Odyssey they honor combat prowess above all (Opie 'went out a warrior' in the prison fight), prize loyalty to comrades and family (Achilles avenging Patroclus as Jax hunts Opie's killer), treat ambush and deception of outsiders as virtues (Odysseus's wooden horse as the bathroom ambush of A.J. Weston), and regard revenge as a moral duty, from Piney's shooting at Laroy to Gemma's 'He's gonna die by the hands of a son.' The parallels cut both ways: Odysseus's torture of Melanthius makes Clay's castration of a child rapist look merciful, while SAMCRO's chapel democracy and protection of Charming soften the heroic contempt for underlings like Thersites. The chapter ends where Greek ethics began — with the question whether the rationalist reaction of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle or the way of the warrior should guide a life.

chapters.file: ch31 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Presents three ancient alternatives to SAMCRO's warrior ethic. Diogenes the Cynic, 'the earliest of all the fathers of anarchy,' matches J.T.'s Harley-commune ideal — reject greed, convention, and wage slavery like Tig punching the clock at Teller-Morrow — but the chapter argues pure anarchy regenerates hierarchy: with no authority, revenge becomes the only justice and 'a big guy like Clay' mugs 'a small guy like Chuckie.' Plato's Republic supplies the reformist pole — impartial justice for all citizens rather than loyalty circles, rulers picked from proven warriors for wisdom (Tara belongs healing, not scheming), family curbed where it breeds Gemma-style favoritism — yet proves too authoritarian, so Aristotle's function argument (reason as the human ergon), virtue, and the three kinds of friendship (SAMCRO's pleasure-friendships, Clay–Unser's usefulness) sketch a livable middle way with duties even to strangers.

holes.name: Paul Ricoeur
holes.what: French philosopher whose Oneself as Another distinguishes idem-identity (sameness) from ipse-identity (selfhood) and argues the self is constituted through narrative, character, and promise keeping.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire analysis of Tara's tattoo, Tig's breakdown, Opie's promises, and John Teller's legacy is built step by step on Ricoeur's theory of narrative identity.

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The thesis that personal identity is constituted by the story a person weaves from sameness, selfhood, character, and promises, given an ethical aim of 'the good life with and for others.'
holes.why: Chapter 21's title is 'Narrative Identity in Charming' and every case in it (Tara, Tig, Opie, SAMCRO itself) is an instance of identity maintained through narrative.

holes.name: Robert Pirsig
holes.what: American author of Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, who treats motorcycle maintenance as caring engagement with technology that overcomes alienation from the mechanical world.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is framed by Pirsig's book and resolves its argument with his claims that technology frightens because it feels like a 'death force' and that repair is a form of care.

holes.name: Hubert Dreyfus
holes.what: Twentieth-century Heideggerian philosopher of mind who argued (with Stuart Dreyfus) that expert skill is pre-reflective, embodied know-how that cannot be captured by rules or AI representations.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Dreyfus's skill theory to explain why Jax's riding, Chibs's brawling, and Tara's surgery work best when conscious self-monitoring disappears.

holes.name: Readiness-to-Hand (Zuhandenheit)
holes.what: Heidegger's analysis of equipment as-transparent-in-use (readiness-to-hand), conspicuous in malfunction (un-readiness-to-hand), or detachedly inspected (presence-at-hand).
holes.why: Chapter 22 organizes the biker's whole relation to the motorcycle around these three modes, from absorbed riding to the roadside breakdown to the parts catalogue.

holes.name: The Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's account of the phallic-stage fixation in which a boy desires his mother and rivals his father, resolved by identification with the father, with lasting effects if unresolved.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central move, via Ernest Jones's Hamlet and Oedipus, is diagnosing Jax's bond with Gemma and rivalry with Clay as an unresolved Oedipus complex.

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French feminist philosopher who argues patriarchal society devalues women, circulates them as commodities exchanged among men, and blocks women from speaking as independent subjects.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is a sustained application of Irigaray (This Sex Which Is Not One, Speculum of the Other Woman) to Gemma and Tara as 'old ladies' in a male-dominated club.

holes.name: The Public and Private Realms
holes.what: Arendt's distinction in The Human Condition between the public political realm where humans appear as truly human and the private domestic realm of necessity, labor, and the life process.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its 'feminine sphere versus masculine sphere' framing of SAMCRO directly on Arendt's public/private distinction and her worry about the collapsing 'social' realm.

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Early modern Italian philosopher of history whose New Science holds that history moves in corsi and recorsi, decaying from imaginative founding through the 'barbarism of reflection' before re-founding.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Vico's cycle to explain SAMCRO's fall from J.T.'s imaginative 1967 founding into Clay's rational greed and the club's near-annihilation.

holes.name: Homer
holes.what: Bronze Age Greek epic poet whose Iliad and Odyssey encode the archaic warrior ethos of honor, glory, loyalty, and revenge that later Greek moral philosophy defined itself against.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire argument maps SAMCRO's outlaw code point by point onto Homeric heroism, from Opie as the warrior to Odysseus's trickery and Achilles's revenge.

holes.name: Warrior Morality (Homeric honor culture)
holes.what: The pre-philosophical ethic of the Iliad and Odyssey in which a good life is measured by combat prowess, glory, loyalty to friends and family, ruthless victory, and revenge as duty.
holes.why: Chapter 30 identifies this warrior ethic as the value system SAMCRO shares with Homer's heroes, the foil against which Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle first reacted.
